title: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND STILL LIVE COMFORTABLY IN SIN?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND STILL LIVE COMFORTABLY IN SIN?
The Most Dangerous Place for a Christian Is Not Where You Fall Into Sin… It’s Where You No Longer Feel the Need to Get Up.
There is something more frightening than a Christian falling into sin.
It is a Christian who has learned how to live there.

Someone who can worship on Sunday, entertain darkness on Monday, quote Scripture on Tuesday, return to a secret addiction on Wednesday, ask God for blessings on Thursday, ignore conviction on Friday, and walk into church on Saturday as though nothing is wrong.
And the most terrifying part?
They no longer feel the contradiction.
Not because God has stopped being holy.
Not because sin has become harmless.
But because a heart can become so accustomed to compromise that what once brought tears of repentance now barely produces a moment of discomfort.
Read that again.
The sin that once broke your heart can eventually become the sin you defend, if you keep silencing the conviction that was meant to bring you home.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question you will face today is not whether you believe in Jesus.
It is whether the Jesus you claim to love has permission to confront the life you have chosen to protect.
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A difference between falling into darkness and furnishing a room there.
A difference between crying out, "Lord, deliver me," and quietly deciding, "Lord, understand me."
One is the desperate struggle of a person who needs grace.
The other may reveal a heart that wants the benefits of a Savior without surrendering to His lordship.
And before you assume this article is about somebody else, consider something.
Judas walked with Jesus.
He heard the sermons. Witnessed the miracles. Shared meals with the disciples. Saw compassion that could silence a crowd and authority that could command a storm.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not mean his heart was surrendered to Jesus.
That should make every one of us examine ourselves.
Because you can be close to Christian things while remaining dangerously distant from Christ.
You can know worship songs without knowing surrender.
You can defend biblical truth online while privately refusing to obey it.
You can be surrounded by people who call you a strong Christian while carrying secrets you have convinced yourself God will never confront.
And you can become so skilled at appearing spiritually healthy that even you begin believing the performance.
But Jesus is not deceived by the version of ourselves we present to the world.
He sees the heart.
He sees what happens after the worship music stops.
He sees what you search for when nobody is watching.
He hears the words you say when anger takes control.

He knows the bitterness you keep feeding, the dishonest choices you keep excusing, the sexual temptation you keep entertaining, the pride you refuse to confess, and the forgiveness you keep withholding.
And still, He calls sinners to come to Him.
Not because sin is acceptable.
But because His mercy is greater than the darkness from which He came to rescue us.
Listen carefully to what Jesus actually said.
In John 14:15, the Greek text reads:
«Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.»
A faithful translation is:
"If you love me, you will keep my commandments."
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) comes from the verb agapaō, meaning to love. The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from tēreō, meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say, "If you love Me, you will never struggle."
He did not say, "If you love Me, you will achieve sinless perfection before you can come near Me."
He connected genuine love with obedience.
In the immediate context, Jesus was comforting His disciples before His departure, promising the Holy Spirit and preparing them for a life of faithful discipleship.
His words were not a formula for earning salvation through flawless behavior.
They described the relationship between love for Christ and a life increasingly shaped by His commands.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase His love. It is a fruit that grows from a life transformed by His grace.
And this is where the question becomes deeply personal.
If Jesus says, "Follow Me," but we continually answer, "Only where it is convenient," what exactly are we following?
If He says, "Forgive," but we treasure revenge, what are we protecting?
If He says, "Flee sexual immorality," but we deliberately arrange opportunities to indulge it, what are we choosing?
If He says, "Repent," but we insist that nothing needs to change, have we truly listened?
There is a kind of Christianity that wants Jesus to remove guilt without confronting the sin that produces it.
It wants peace without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Blessing without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
A Savior who comforts, but never corrects.
But the Jesus revealed in Scripture cannot be reduced to a comforting accessory for a life we refuse to surrender.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
And His grace does not merely pardon sinners.
It teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 declares that the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and training believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Think about that.
Grace trains us.
Grace does not give us permission to remain enslaved to what Christ died to redeem us from.
Grace meets us in our brokenness, forgives us through Christ, and begins transforming our desires, decisions, and direction.
This is why the apostle Paul asked a question that still cuts through centuries of religious excuses.
Romans 6:1–2, in the original Greek, begins:
«Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ; μὴ γένοιτο.»
Translated:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? Certainly not!"
The phrase μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito) is an emphatic rejection.
Paul is not mildly suggesting that continuing in sin might be unwise.
He is forcefully rejecting the idea that God's grace should be used as an excuse to continue in sin.
And the context matters.
Romans 6 explains that believers have been united with Christ in His death and resurrection. Because they belong to Him, sin is no longer to reign over their mortal bodies.
Paul does not teach that Christians become incapable of sinning.
He teaches that sin must no longer be treated as their rightful master.
Jesus did not die so you could become comfortable in your chains. He died and rose again so sin would no longer have the final claim over your life.
Imagine a prisoner sitting in a dark cell.
For years, he has begged for freedom.
He has wept over the iron bars, the locked door, the hopelessness of captivity.
Then one day, someone comes.
The debt is paid.
The door is opened.
The chains fall.
The prisoner is invited to walk into the light.
But instead of leaving, he begins decorating the cell.
He hangs pictures on the walls.
He makes the bed more comfortable.
He tells himself that captivity is not so terrible after all.
And when someone asks why he remains, he says, "Because I know I'm free."
That is the contradiction Paul is confronting.
Freedom in Christ is not freedom to embrace the slavery from which He has delivered us.
It is freedom to belong to Him.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because somewhere, someone reading this is not comfortable in sin at all.
You are exhausted by it.
You have prayed about the same weakness so many times that you are ashamed to pray again.
You have made promises you failed to keep.
You have cried after another relapse.
You have wondered whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
You have asked yourself whether a genuine Christian could possibly struggle as much as you do.
And perhaps this article has made your chest tighten because you are afraid that your failures prove you never loved Jesus.
Please hear this distinction.
A Christian who hates their sin but continues fighting against it is not in the same spiritual condition as someone who deliberately cherishes sin and refuses repentance.
That does not make repeated sin harmless.
Nor does feeling guilty automatically prove genuine repentance.
But Scripture does not tell broken believers to wait until they become perfect before approaching Christ.
First John 1:8 says that if we claim to have no sin, we deceive ourselves.
And the very next verse offers astonishing hope.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
John writes these words to believers.
People who still need confession.
People who still need cleansing.
People whose relationship with God is grounded not in their own perfection, but in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Then, in 1 John 2:1, he explains that he writes so believers will not sin, but if anyone does sin, Jesus Christ the righteous is their advocate with the Father.
Do you see the beauty of that balance?
Do not sin.
But if you sin, do not run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him in repentance and faith.
Because the same Christ who calls you to holiness is the Christ who intercedes for His people.
He is not indifferent to your sin.
And He is not unwilling to receive the repentant sinner.
That is the Gospel.
Not a message that says your sin does not matter.
But the breathtaking announcement that your sin was serious enough to require the cross, and God's love was great enough to give His Son.
Now consider Peter.
A man who genuinely loved Jesus.
A man who had witnessed His glory.
A man who boldly declared his loyalty.
And yet, when fear tightened its grip, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 records that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The cold night.
The fading echoes of his own denial.
And then the eyes of Jesus.
The One Peter had promised never to abandon.
The One he had just denied.
Scripture does not tell us everything Peter saw in that look.
We should not pretend to know every emotion that passed between them.
But we do know what happened next.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
And his story was not over.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, beside the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
But notice something crucial.
Jesus did not restore Peter by declaring that denial was acceptable.
He restored him into a life of renewed love, obedience, and service.
Grace did not erase the seriousness of Peter's failure. Grace ensured that Peter's failure would not be the final chapter of his story.
From shame to restoration.
From denial to discipleship.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to understand.
Your worst failure does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your hidden sin does not have to remain your secret prison.
Your past does not have the authority to cancel the future Christ is calling you into.
But you cannot embrace His restoration while insisting on protecting the very sin He is calling you to surrender.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after being caught.
It is not simply crying because consequences have arrived.
And it is not promising change just long enough for the guilt to disappear.
The New Testament commonly uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, associated with a change of mind and understanding that involves turning toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely a passing emotion.
It is a real reorientation of the heart and life toward God, producing fruit consistent with that change.
That does not mean every sinful habit disappears instantly.
Some battles involve years of growth, accountability, wise counsel, prayer, practical boundaries, and persistent dependence on the Holy Spirit.
But repentance stops defending the enemy.
It stops calling darkness light.
It stops treating God's patience as permission.
And when it falls, it returns to the Savior instead of building a theology to excuse the fall.
There is an Old Testament passage that beautifully captures the seriousness of this surrender.
Ezekiel 36:26 contains God's promise:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ
Ve-natatti lakhem lev chadash.
"And I will give you a new heart."
In its original context, this promise was given to Israel as part of God's promised restoration, including cleansing, a new heart, and the gift of His Spirit.
It must not be stripped from that covenant setting.
Yet the wider biblical story reveals the significance of God's transforming work, fulfilled through the new covenant established by Jesus Christ.
God does not merely demand external improvement.
He acts to renew His people from within.
And that is something human willpower alone cannot accomplish.
You can delete an app and still desire the sin.
You can avoid a person and still nurture bitterness.
You can stop saying certain words while pride continues ruling your heart.
You can change your surroundings without surrendering your affections.
External boundaries are valuable.
Sometimes they are absolutely necessary.
But the deepest transformation is not merely behavioral management.
It is the work of God renewing a human heart.
That is why you need more than motivation.
You need Christ.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need the Word of God to confront the lies you have believed.
You need a community of faithful believers who will love you enough to encourage you and tell you the truth.
And sometimes you need to make a painful decision that your old self would never have made.
End the relationship that continually draws you into disobedience.
Confess the deception.
Return what you dishonestly took.
Seek forgiveness from the person you wounded.
Get help for the addiction you keep hiding.
Put boundaries around the temptations you have been deliberately feeding.
Not because these actions earn God's forgiveness.
But because repentance bears fruit.
And because loving Jesus involves learning to say no to the things that pull your heart away from Him.
Jesus used startling language in Matthew 5:29–30 about removing whatever causes one to sin.
In context, He was emphasizing the radical seriousness with which sin must be addressed, not commanding literal self-injury.
The point is unmistakable.
Do not make comfortable arrangements with what is destroying you.
Some doors need to be closed.
Some habits need to be abandoned.
Some secrets need to be brought into the light.
And some excuses need to die before the life you keep praying for can begin taking shape.
But perhaps the greatest danger is not that you have committed a terrible sin.
Perhaps it is that you have become so accustomed to it that you no longer want to change.
Hebrews 3:13 warns believers about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
That word deceitfulness matters.
Sin does not usually introduce itself by announcing that it intends to destroy your fellowship with God, damage your relationships, and dull your conscience.
It whispers.
"Just this once."
"Everyone does it."
"You deserve this."
"God knows your heart."
"You can repent tomorrow."
And tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes next year.
The conscience grows quieter.
The excuses grow louder.
And eventually the person who once trembled at the thought of dishonoring Christ begins defending the very things they once begged Him to remove.
That is why a comfortable relationship with unrepentant sin is spiritually dangerous.
Not because one failure places a repentant believer beyond God's mercy.
But because persistent, willing rebellion against Christ contradicts the profession that He is Lord.
First John 3:6–10 speaks forcefully about the incompatibility between abiding in Christ and an ongoing pattern of lawlessness.
These verses must be read alongside 1 John 1:8–2:2, where the same apostle acknowledges believers' continuing need for forgiveness and Christ's advocacy.
John is not contradicting himself.
He is distinguishing the life characterized by fellowship with God from a life characterized by persistent, unrepentant rebellion.
And we should not use those passages to make final judgments about every struggling person's salvation.
God knows the heart.
But neither should we soften John's warning until it loses its force.
A faith that continually makes peace with what Jesus calls sin deserves serious examination, not automatic reassurance.
Second Corinthians 13:5 tells believers to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith.
That is not an invitation to endless despair.
It is an invitation to spiritual honesty.
So ask yourself.
When was the last time God's Word changed a decision you were determined to make?
When was the last time you confessed something without waiting to be exposed?
When was the last time you chose obedience even though disobedience promised immediate pleasure?
When was the last time you stopped explaining away a sin and simply admitted, "Lord, You are right, and I am wrong"?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
Is there something in your life you are asking Jesus to bless that He is actually calling you to leave behind?
Stay with that question for a moment.
Do not rush to another notification.
Do not immediately search your mind for someone who needs to read this more than you.
Allow the Word of God to examine you first.
Because this is not about winning an argument over whether a Christian can sin.
Every Christian still needs grace.
This is about whether we are willing to let the grace of God change us.
And the answer to the title's question must be given carefully.
Can you love Jesus and still struggle with sin?
Yes.
Peter did.
The apostle John acknowledged that believers still sin.
Christians continue to battle the flesh, and sanctification remains a lifelong work of God.
But can you genuinely love Jesus while deliberately making sin your settled home, refusing His correction, rejecting repentance, and insisting that His commands have no claim upon your life?
Scripture gives no assurance to a heart determined to remain in rebellion.
That is not a declaration that every person in such a condition is beyond salvation.
It is a warning not to confuse a profession of love with a surrendered life.
Jesus Himself asked in Luke 6:46:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" — KJV
That question still stands.
And no amount of religious activity can make it disappear.
But neither does Jesus leave the repentant sinner standing in hopelessness.
Remember the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15.
The younger son took his inheritance, departed into a distant country, and squandered what he had been given.
Eventually, his choices brought him to hunger, humiliation, and desperation.
Then Luke 15:17 records a turning point.
He came to himself.
He recognized his condition.
He resolved to return to his father.
He did not arrive with a résumé of accomplishments.
He came confessing his sin and acknowledging his unworthiness.
And while he was still a long way off, his father saw him, felt compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
Do not miss the beauty.
The father did not celebrate the rebellion.
He celebrated the return.
The son did not earn his way back into the father's compassion.
He was received with astonishing mercy.
And in the parable, the father declares that his son was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found.
Jesus told this story in a context where religious leaders were complaining that He welcomed sinners.
The parable reveals the joy surrounding repentance and the extraordinary mercy of God toward the lost.
It is not permission to remain in the far country.
It is an invitation to come home.
And maybe that is where this article has found you.
In a far country nobody else knows about.
You still smile in church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still say, "God is good."
But inside, something has grown distant.
The joy you once knew feels faint.
Prayer has become difficult because honesty would require confronting what you have been avoiding.
You have learned how to distract yourself from conviction.
And you wonder whether you have wandered too far.
Hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow when you feel stronger.
Not after you have manufactured a perfect record.
Not when you finally become worthy of His attention.
Come in repentance and faith.
Bring the truth.
Bring the shame.
Bring the failures.
Bring the secret you are afraid to name.
Bring the habit you have tried to defeat in your own strength.
Bring the broken promises.
Bring the exhausted heart.
You do not have to pretend that your sin is small.
And you do not have to pretend that Christ's mercy is small either.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love for us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
The cross is not proof that God overlooks sin.
It is proof that God has acted decisively to save sinners through the sacrifice of His Son.
Jesus bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is invited to receive forgiveness and new life.
You cannot save yourself through religious performance.
You cannot wash away your guilt by accumulating enough good deeds.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not the result of works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
But Ephesians 2:10 also reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves.
Grace transforms.
Grace produces a life increasingly shaped by love and obedience.
That is the difference.
You do not obey Jesus so that He might become willing to save you.
You obey because the Savior who has shown you mercy is worthy of your love, trust, and surrender.
And even when you stumble, you return to Him.
Again.
With honesty.
With repentance.
With faith.
With the willingness to take the next obedient step.
Perhaps today that step is a confession.
Perhaps it is seeking help.
Perhaps it is breaking off a sinful arrangement.
Perhaps it is asking someone to pray with you.
Perhaps it is returning to the Scriptures after months of spiritual neglect.
Or perhaps it is simply getting on your knees and saying words you have avoided for far too long.

"Lord Jesus, I have been calling You my Savior while resisting You as my Lord. I have excused what You have called sin. I have hidden what You have called me to confess. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot transform my own heart. I need Your grace, Your truth, and the power of Your Holy Spirit. Lead me in genuine repentance. Restore my love for You. Help me walk in obedience, not to earn Your salvation, but because You alone are worthy. Amen."
And if those words reflect what is happening in your heart, do not let this moment disappear beneath another hour of scrolling.
Tell the truth.
Not for applause.
Not to prove your spirituality to strangers.
But because sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the beginning of refusing to let shame rule the conversation.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from compromise into repentance, consider sharing it. Someone reading the comments may need to know that failure does not have to be the end.
You do not need to disclose intimate details publicly. God hears even the prayer you cannot bring yourself to write.
But do not underestimate what an honest testimony can mean to another struggling soul.
Someone may be sitting in a parked car tonight, staring at their phone, wondering whether they should finally return to Jesus.
Someone may have convinced themselves that because they have fallen so many times, getting up no longer matters.
Not everyone will agree with it.
Some may feel uncomfortable.
But perhaps one person will stop long enough to open a Bible, confess a sin, seek help, or pray for the first time in years.

Invite your friends, your family, struggling believers, those who have grown lukewarm, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along. Not because a social media page can replace the local church, personal Bible study, prayer, or Christian fellowship, but because faithful Gospel-centered encouragement can help point people toward those essential parts of discipleship.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior.
Behind every article is a desire to see more people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
We want to keep reaching the weary believer.
The person quietly battling sin.
The young Christian hungry for sound teaching.
The wounded soul who has mistaken shame for the voice of God.
The family looking for biblical encouragement.
And the person who has never truly understood why Jesus died and rose again.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not driven by pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
There are many ways to honor Christ through generosity, service, prayer, and faithful stewardship.
These are simply practical gifts of appreciation, not measures of anyone's faith or spiritual standing.
The goal is not merely to produce more content.
It is to help people engage with Scripture, grow in biblical understanding, and develop a deeper, more faithful walk with Jesus.
Your generosity is appreciated.
Your prayers matter.
And your willingness to share biblical truth may reach someone we could never reach on our own.
But above all, remember this.
Jesus Christ is the reason for everything.
Not the platform.
Not the numbers.
Not the recognition.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers when others withdrew.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners when others condemned them.
The One who spoke truth without compromise and offered mercy without pretending sin was harmless.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And the One who can take a life that appears hopelessly stained by failure and begin writing a testimony of grace.
So return to the question that brought you here.
Can you love Jesus and still live comfortably in sin?

If by comfort you mean deliberately cherishing sin, refusing repentance, and dismissing His authority while expecting assurance that everything is spiritually well, Scripture will not give you that reassurance.
But if you mean that you love Jesus, hate the sin that keeps entangling you, and sometimes fall while sincerely longing to follow Him, do not mistake your battle for proof that His mercy has run out.
Keep coming to Christ.
Keep confessing.
Keep seeking help.
Keep turning from what dishonors Him.
Keep trusting His finished work rather than your own performance.
Because your hope is not that you will become strong enough to stop needing grace.
Your hope is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior, and His Spirit is at work in those who belong to Him.
One day, when the battle is finally over and God's people are made perfect in His presence, sin will no longer wound their fellowship with Him.
Until then, we walk by faith.
We repent.
We obey.
We grow.
We sometimes stumble.
And by God's grace, we rise again.
Not because sin is a small thing.
But because Jesus is a mighty Savior.
And maybe the miracle you need today is not another emotional experience.
Maybe it is the courage to stop defending what is hurting you and finally surrender it to the One who died to save you.
The most heartbreaking tragedy is not that you fell into the darkness… it is that the door to grace stood open, and you became too comfortable to walk toward the Light.
